newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal coalition faces close confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Nepal coalition faces close confidence vote.

text.p: Nepal's week-old governing coalition linking former royalists and communists faces its first test in a confidence vote on Wednesday afternoon that is expected to be a close call.

Prime Minister Lokendra Bahadur Chand took power in the world's only Hindu kingdom last week after a 17-month-old centre-right coalition, undermined by charges of corruption, narrowly lost a vote of confidence.
Chand leads a group of rebel legislators from the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), which helped topple the previous government.

"Obviously the government believes it has enough support," said a parliament official. "But recent trends have indicated mounting uncertainty about what really could happen on the floor of the house."

The RPP's leaders helped rule the country during nearly three decades of party-less government from 1961 to 1990 that was dominated by King Birendra. Under that system, the monarch enjoyed absolute power to select and dismiss prime ministers.
The king bowed to pro-democracy demonstrators in 1990 and ushered in multi-party democracy.
The badly split parliament that emerged from general elections in late 1994 has yielded three coalition governments.
Chand joined with the communist Unified Marxist-Leninist (UML) party, the biggest single party in the lower house of parliament, to topple the previous government and stake a claim to power.
Chand is required by law to prove his majority in parliament within 30 days of taking office.

His RPP faction has 10 seats in the 205-member lower house and the UML 90. Counting other partners, the coalition commands 114 votes, enough to win the vote of confidence that parliament officials said was set for Wednesday afternoon.
The opposition Nepali Congress party holds 86 seats with the rest controlled by independent members.
If he wins the vote, Chand was expected to quickly expand his eight-member cabinet, with communists likely to receive three out of every five portfolios, officials said.

The major parties differ little over policy, but the communists were expected to slow economic liberalisation. The UML braked privatisation during the nine months it held power after the 1994 elections.
